summary: The Moon’s south pole presents unique challenges for lunar exploration.  Limited sunlight, complex terrain and restricted Earth visibility can significantly affect mission operations and landing site planning. LunarNav is an intuitive web application designed to compare 31 potential landing sites across the Lunar South Pole plus Apollo 11. By integrating NASA scientific data with interactive visualizations, our project helps users identify favourable illumination and direct to Earth visibility windows while exploring how conditions evolve over time. When mission schedules change or landing dates are delayed, Lunar Navigator enables users to quickly reassess site conditions and explore alternative locations that better align with mission requirements. By transforming complex scientific data into clear, LunarNav simplifies preliminary lunar mission planning and makes lunar exploration more accessible to both space professionals and the general public.
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work ?

LunarNav is an interactive web application forcomparing 31 landing sites near the Moon’s south pole, plus Apollo 11 as an equatorial reference. Users can explore solar illumination and direct-to-Earth geometric visibility across different dates, examine site conditions and assess how changes to an expected landing date affect the available operational windows. The user-facing scenario covers November 15, 2026 through November 15, 2030. The application brings together NASA JPL Horizons ephemerides, NASA LOLA topographic data and a curated site catalogue. An offline processing pipeline prepares site-specific terrain horizons and time-dependent results. The application then uses these precomputed datasets to respond rapidly to site, date and mission-duration selections.

2. Moon orbit

For each site, the model converts latitude and longitude into a three-dimensional local reference frame. Apparent Sun and Earth directions are then expressed as azimuth (compass bearing) and elevation (angle above the ideal horizon). These coordinates provide the geometric basis for the visibility calculations. Sun and Earth positions are downloaded hourly from JPL Horizons in the Moon Mean Earth frame, and match independent Horizons queries to within 0.006°.

3. How the local terrain changes visibility

The NASA LOLA digital elevation model is represented in a polar stereographic grid. The application interpolates terrain heights bilinearly and casts rays in 80 m steps out to 250 km around the site, from an observer 2 m or 10 m above the ground to estimate the local horizon at 720 azimuths, spaced 0.5° apart. The resulting horizon profile captures the possibility that a ridge blocks the Sun or Earth even when the object lies above the ideal, unobstructed horizon.

4. Visible results

Because the terrain skyline may cut across the apparent solar or terrestrial disk, the model estimates the fraction of that disk lying above the horizon. It splits the disk into 16 vertical strips, each compared with the skyline at its own azimuth using the exact circular-segment area.” Add at the end: “The Sun counts as up when its upper edge clears the terrain, and its apparent size follows its distance. This supports a more nuanced illustration of partial occultation than a center-point-only test.

5. What benefits does it provide ?

The main benefit is rapid, understandable comparison. Instead of combining separate topographic, astronomical and numerical products by hand, users can explore how sites differ in sunlight and potential direct-to-Earth visibility. A shift in the planned landing date can be reassessed, making it easier to identify alternatives that better match stated mission constraints.

The interface is intended for both specialists performing preliminary screening and non-specialists learning why the Lunar South Pole is a challenging environment. Prepared datasets keep demanding computations out of the interactive workflow, while the public web deployment makes the experience easier to access.

6. What is the intended impact ?

The lunar south pole is a focus of scientific exploration in part because permanently shadowed terrain may preserve water ice and other volatile materials. Illumination and geometric Earth visibility are relevant to early mission planning, especially when operations or schedules change. Lunar Navigator aims to make those environmental trade-offs easier to interpret and communicate, without claiming to certify landing safety, energy sufficiency or radio-link performance.

7. What technologies and software were used ?

The technical documentation identifies NASA JPL Horizons API for time-dependent Sun/Earth information; NASA PDS LOLA for terrain; C# and .NET / ASP.NET for scientific and API components; and Blazor for the web interface. GitHub manages code changes. Docker and Render are used for deployment, and Swagger documents the API and lets users test its endpoints.

The deployment diagram shows a two-stage Docker build and run process. After changes are merged into the main branch, Render rebuilds and redeploys the API. The packaged application includes data files and a DEM downloaded from NASA PDS, used for custom points, with a health-check endpoint for basic availability. NASA JPL Horizons API : (fetched with a Python scripts).

8. How is the project creative ?

LunarNav’s creative contribution is not the invention of new ephemeris or terrain measurements. It is the integration of complex scientific information into a site-by-date decision experience that lets users see what changes when their mission plans change. Combining interactive comparisons with terrain-aware, partial-disk visibility estimates helps bridge detailed scientific calculation and accessible interpretation.

The central message is simple: we turn complex lunar data into clear, decision-relevant insights, while allowing users to understand the physical causes behind the results.

9. What factors did the team consider ?

Scientific factors include local topography, azimuth, elevation, terrain masking, observation height, partial disk visibility and the evolution of Sun/Earth geometry over time. Engineering factors include preprocessing time, stored dataset size, fast interactive calculations, API availability and a deployment pipeline. User-experience factors include accessible terminology, clear comparisons, understandable caveats and responsiveness.

The project’s glossary defines a digital elevation model (DEM), a horizon mask, the apparent disk fraction, a mission stay and the effect of a schedule slip. It also distinguishes geometric Earth visibility from a guaranteed radio connection. These definitions support transparent interpretation of results. The results were validated against NASA Goddard’s PGDA illumination maps: 26 of 31 sites agree within 5 percentage points for the Sun and 28 of 31 for the Earth, with a median difference under 1 point.
